text.p: These are the stories making headlines in the Namibian press on Tuesday. Retuers has not verifired these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Giving the clearest indication yet that government will not be deterred from powering ahead with the controversial Epupa dam, President Sam Nujoma said the pre-feasibility studies show the hydro-electric scheme is "both technically and financially" viable.

- The government of Rwanda has requested the extradition of Dr Andre Rwamakuba, a Rwandan working in Namibia. Dr Ben Karenzi, non-resident ambassador to Namibia says his government has extensive evidence that Rwamakuba was involved in genocide activities.

- The Namibian Law Association has noted with "deep concern" the behaviour of members of the police, who allegedly stopped members of the Legal Assistence Centre from meeting with its clients at Epupa.

- Dr Andre Rwamakuba, the controversial Rwandan, sought by his government for acts of genocide, cannot be extradited directly to the Rwandan government for lack of an extradition treaty between Namibia and Rwanda.

- Just two days after the announcement that a new political party is to be formed in Namibia, the president of the Namibia Movement for Independent Candidates (NMIC), Joseph Kauandenge, has received his first death threat.

- The ministry of health and social services has been buying millions of dollars worth of unregistered medicines since Dr Libertine Amathila took charge of the ministry last year it has been confirmed by several well-informed sources, who wished to remain anonymous.

- Don Todd, who undertook aircraft accident investigations within the directorate of civil aviation prior to the crash of a Cessna 210 in the Naukluft mountains earlier this year, has apologised to the families of the victims for not having been assertive enough in his investigation efforts.
